lead: A point-to-point link is one transmitter, one fiber path and one receiver, with only splices and connectors between them: a trunk between two telephone exchanges, a cable-TV headend feeding a street node, a run between two buildings. Digital and analog links use the same blocks. A digital link is judged by how many bits arrive wrong, an analog link by how much noise rides on the waveform, and that difference decides what the receiver is designed for.
prereq: You need optical sources (LED and laser), photodetectors and responsivity, and receiver noise and bit error rate.

sections.h3: The blocks of a point-to-point link

blocks.text: Both link types use the same chain of blocks.

items: Driver and source. An LED or laser diode and the circuit that drives it: current pulses for a digital link, a bias plus a varying signal current for an analog one. The output is the mean launched power PT in dBm.
Fiber, splices and connectors. The cable loses αL dB (α in dB/km, L in km); each joint adds a fixed loss.
Photodiode. A pin photodiode or avalanche photodiode (APD) turns received power P into current Ip = ℛP, with ℛ the responsivity in A/W.
Preamplifier and filter. Raises the current and limits the bandwidth B, which sets how much noise passes.
Decision circuit or measurement stage. A digital receiver samples each bit and decides 1 or 0; an analog receiver keeps the waveform, measured for carrier-to-noise ratio.

blocks.text: Every loss before the photodiode lowers the current, but the preamplifier's thermal noise does not shrink with it, so received power is the first thing a design checks.

A digital link design starts from three requirements: the bit rate B in bit/s, the distance L in km, and the bit error rate (BER) the user will accept. BER is the fraction of bits decided wrongly. A target of 10⁻⁹ at 2.5 Gbit/s still means 2.5 errors every second, so faster links ask for 10⁻¹² or use error-correcting codes.
The designer then chooses the parts; some syllabi call these the system considerations:

head: Choice
Options
What decides it
rows: Fiber loss and dispersion there; cost of parts
Multimode (50 or 62.5 µm core) or single-mode
Distance and bit rate: only multimode has modal dispersion
Coupled power, spectral width, rise time
Sensitivity: an APD gains about 5 to 10 dB but needs a high bias

blocks.text: An 850 nm LED on multimode fiber with a silicon pin detector is cheapest for a few kilometres at tens of Mbit/s; a 1310 nm laser on single-mode fiber covers tens of kilometres; a 1550 nm DFB laser with an APD or amplifier covers long spans.

Every design then faces two checks. The link power budget asks whether enough light arrives. The rise-time budget asks whether the pulses are still sharp enough. The link works only if it passes both.

sections.h3: Analog links: modulation index and carrier-to-noise ratio

blocks.text: In an analog link the light intensity follows the signal: the laser is biased at a steady power and the signal swings it up and down, so the source must be linear. The modulation index m is the peak deviation of the power from its mean, divided by the mean: a swing from 0.5P to 1.5P is m = 0.5, not 1.
The photocurrent has a mean I<sub>p</sub> = ℛP and a signal of peak mI<sub>p</sub>, whose mean-square value is (mI<sub>p</sub>)²/2. Three noises add, each a mean-square current in A²:
CNR = ½(m ℛ P)² ÷ [ RIN·(ℛP)²·B + 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>D</sub>)B + 4k<sub>B</sub>TBF<sub>t</sub>/R<sub>eq</sub> ]
blocks.where: P is mean received power in W; RIN is the laser's relative intensity noise per Hz (−143 dB/Hz = 10<sup>−14.3</sup>/Hz); B is bandwidth in Hz; q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; I<sub>D</sub> is dark current; k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K; T in K; F<sub>t</sub> is the preamplifier noise figure as a ratio; R<sub>eq</sub> is the load in Ω. CNR(dB) = 10 log₁₀ CNR.

blocks.text: RIN noise grows as P², like the signal, so it sets a CNR ceiling that more power cannot lift. Shot noise grows as P, so a shot-limited CNR changes 10 dB per 10 dB of power. Thermal noise does not depend on P, so a thermal-limited CNR changes 20 dB per 10 dB. A cable-TV channel needs about 50 dB.

When many channels ride on separate subcarriers, the laser's nonlinearity mixes them: two-carrier beats are quoted as composite second order (CSO), three-carrier beats as composite triple beat (CTB). They fall inside other channels and no filter removes them, so m per channel is kept to a few percent.

examples.question: An analog video link uses a laser with RIN = −143 dB/Hz. The receiver has a pin photodiode of responsivity 0.6 A/W, negligible dark current, an equivalent load of 750 Ω and a preamplifier noise figure of 3 dB, at T = 300 K. The channel bandwidth is 6 MHz and the modulation index is m = 0.5. (a) For a received power of −10 dBm, find each noise term and the CNR in dB. (b) Find the CNR if the received power falls to −20 dBm, and say which noise limits each case.
steps: Received power: P = 10<sup>−10/10</sup> mW = 0.1 mW = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ W. Photocurrent I<sub>p</sub> = ℛP = 0.6 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ A = 60 µA.
Signal power: ½(mI<sub>p</sub>)² = ½ × (0.5 × 6.0 × 10⁻⁵)² = ½ × (3.0 × 10⁻⁵)² = 4.50 × 10⁻¹⁰ A². (The RMS signal current is 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ √2 = 21.2 µA.)
RIN noise: RIN = 10<sup>−14.3</sup> = 5.01 × 10⁻¹⁵ per Hz. RIN·I<sub>p</sub>²·B = 5.01 × 10⁻¹⁵ × (6.0 × 10⁻⁵)² × 6 × 10⁶ = 1.08 × 10⁻¹⁶ A².
Total noise = 1.08 + 1.15 + 2.65 = 4.88 × 10⁻¹⁶ A². CNR = 4.50 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 4.88 × 10⁻¹⁶ = 9.22 × 10⁵, so CNR = 10 log₁₀(9.22 × 10⁵) = 59.6 dB. Thermal noise is the largest of the three.
(b) At −20 dBm, I<sub>p</sub> = 6.0 µA. Signal and RIN fall 100 times (4.50 × 10⁻¹² and 1.08 × 10⁻¹⁸ A²), shot noise 10 times (1.15 × 10⁻¹⁷ A²); thermal noise stays at 2.65 × 10⁻¹⁶ A².
examples.answer: (a) CNR = 59.6 dB, with thermal noise the largest term. (b) CNR = 42.1 dB: 10 dB less light cost 17.5 dB, because the receiver is now almost purely thermal-noise limited, and a 50 dB video target is missed.

traps: dBm is optical power: convert to watts before multiplying by ℛ.
Signal power is ½(mI<sub>p</sub>)²; leaving out the ½ makes the CNR 3 dB too high.
Noises add as mean-square currents (A²), never as currents.
CNR is a power ratio: use 10 log₁₀. Using 20 log₁₀ doubles the dB value.
More power does not cure RIN, CSO or CTB.

quiz.q: Which measure judges a digital link and which judges an analog link?
quiz.a: BER for a digital link; carrier-to-noise ratio (together with CSO and CTB for multichannel links) for an analog link.

quiz.q: Why does an analog link need a more linear source than a digital link?
quiz.a: The intensity must copy the waveform, so any curvature distorts it and creates beats between subcarriers; a digital link needs only two clear levels.

quiz.q: A receiver gets −13 dBm and its photodiode has a responsivity of 0.8 A/W. Find the mean photocurrent.
A channel has m = 0.5, a mean photocurrent of 10 µA and a total RMS noise current of 10 nA. Find the CNR in dB.
quiz.a: Signal power ½(0.5 × 10 µA)² = 12.5 µA². Noise power (0.01 µA)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ µA². CNR = 1.25 × 10⁵, that is 51.0 dB.

quiz.q: A link's CNR rises by only 0.5 dB when the received power is raised by 3 dB. What limits it, and what would you change?
quiz.a: Thermal-limited CNR would rise 6 dB and shot-limited 3 dB; a 0.5 dB rise means the noise grows almost as fast as the signal, which is laser RIN. Use a lower-RIN laser, or raise m if distortion allows.

quiz.q: A digital link meets its BER at 20 km but fails when extended to 40 km. Give two possible causes and how you would tell them apart.
quiz.a: Extra loss may push the received power below sensitivity, or dispersion may close the eye. Measure the received power at 40 km: if it is still above sensitivity, dispersion is the cause.

beyond: Cable-TV fiber nodes still quote CNR, CSO and CTB, and radio-over-fiber links carry mobile radio signals to remote antennas, though newer networks digitise closer to the antenna. Search for radio-over-fiber link budget to go further.
